item.title: Yankees' Jazz Chisholm Jr makes wild admission about costly error as team faces postseason elimination
item.description: Jazz Chisholm Jr. airmailed a costly throw in the New York Yankees' ALDS Game 2 loss and admitted he'd still make the same play all over again.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees face an all-too-familiar 2-0 deficit in the postseason, largely due to an all-too-familiar mind-numbing facet of the team.

The Yanks committed three errors in the first four batters of the bottom of the first inning in Game 2 of the American League Division Series on Monday night, and one of them was the result of an additional mental error that's not in the box score.

In an attempt to make a highlight-reel double play that had no chance of being turned, second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. airmailed a throw that brought in the first run.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

It has long been said that there is a lack of accountability in the Yankees' clubhouse, and that appeared to be the case postgame with Chisholm.

When asked if he'd "hold" the ball if he had to do it all over again, Chisholm showed no regrets.

"Honestly, I'd probably still throw it," he admitted without hesitation. "The play was trying to be made. I just feel like I could have probably tried to make an even better throw."

And if it were to happen again, Chisholm has an easy solution.

"Where I'd throw it, I'd try and throw it a little more closer to the base," he said.

RAYS CAPITALIZE ON FOUR YANKEES ERRORS TO TAKE COMMANDING 2-0 ALDS LEAD

Likely Cy Young Award winner Cam Schlittler did not have his best stuff, striking out only two batters while allowing hard-hit contact throughout the night, but the defense did him zero favors. Later in the first, Chisholm also threw a potential double-play ball high.

Chisholm's quote came roughly 24 hours after catcher Austin Wells seemed to have no regrets about making the final out at third by attempting to stretch an eighth-inning double, the Yankees' first and only hit of Game 1, into a triple.

"You have to take risks," Wells said.

The Yanks scored their only runs of Game 2 via two Ben Rice solo homers, while the Rays took advantage of shoddy Yankees defense and timely hitting to win, 5-2.

The series heads to the Bronx on Wednesday night, where the Yankees need to win three in a row to avoid yet another early exit and come within one year of tying their longest championship drought since 1923.

item.title: Dad vanishes on trip with friend to see Cleveland Browns game; police call case 'concerning'
item.description: Phoenix Phillips, 24, vanished in downtown Cleveland hours after watching the Pittsburgh Steelers play. Police call the circumstances "concerning."
item.content:encoded:

item.title: France explodes again as students riot over education
item.description: Video from France Tuesday shows protesters clashing with police and dodging tear gas as tens of thousands demand sweeping education reform nationwide.
item.content:encoded:
Violent scenes are emerging from France Tuesday as tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets to demand education reform, forcing the reported closure of more than half of the country's high schools.

France's interior ministry said 6,100 people have been taken into custody since the protests began in September, while at least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured in clashes, according to Reuters.

Video taken in cities including Paris, Lyon and Strasbourg showed demonstrators facing off with police, lighting fires and dodging tear gas. In other areas such as Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up signs with messages like, "The state has killed national education," Reuters reported.

The Interior Ministry estimated that 86,000 people took part in demonstrations outside Paris on Tuesday morning. More were gathering in the capital for a protest scheduled for the afternoon.

"What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social.

TEEN'S HAND BLOWN OFF BY POLICE GRENADE DURING FRENCH STUDENT PROTESTS: REPORT

Authorities began shutting schools last week to try to diffuse tensions after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry. The High School Students Union also told Reuters that over half of France's high schools were closed or blockaded Tuesday.

Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats.

Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students’ compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.

"We want more money for the national educational system so that high schools are renovated," Roberta, a recent high school graduate in Paris, told Reuters.

FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE

In one of the recent demonstrations on Monday, a 15-year-old had picked up a police dispersal grenade that detonated in the town of Lens, losing his hand and part of his lower arm, officials said.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has asked ministers in France to address student demands including repairs to aging buildings, a call for longer lunch breaks and a review of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day, according to Reuters.

Felix Barney, a university student, told The Associated Press that the police response as disproportionate.

"It doesn’t have any sense to hit minors," he said.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez on Tuesday defended policing methods used against high schoolers, saying the police response has been proportionate in "almost all cases."

Fox News Digital's Louis Casiano and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Blue city emerges as 'suspected hotspot' of visa fraud as swing state lawmaker demands answers
item.description: First on Fox, a blue city in battleground Georgia faces H-1B visa fraud allegations as Rep. Rich McCormick urges a Trump administration probe.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: A blue city in one of the country's hottest battleground states is accused of being a potential hotbed of foreign worker visa fraud, according to the House lawmaker who represents the area.

Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., is writing to the Trump administration on Tuesday asking for an investigation into alleged abuse of the H-1B work visa program in his own district. He warned in the letter that his district is a "suspected hotspot of this fraud" and offered himself as "an interlocutor to help enable cooperation with state-level agencies and law enforcement."

Georgia's 7th Congressional District, which McCormick represents, encompasses part of the Atlanta metro area including the city's northern suburbs. That includes part of Fulton County, whose top prosecutor, Fani Willis, has been under heavy scrutiny by Republicans in recent years.

FEDERAL JUDGE STRIKES DOWN TRUMP’S $100K H-1B VISA FEE, RULING IT AN UNCONSTITUTIONAL TAX

"Established by the Immigration Act of 1990, the purpose of the H-1B program is to allow American businesses to temporarily bring in foreign citizens to fill key, high-skill employment positions when the domestic workforce demonstrably cannot provide the necessary labor," McCormick wrote.

"Unfortunately, the H-1B program has become the subject of rampant fraud and abuse for the nefarious purposes of obtaining labor that bad actors can exploit below-market-rate wages and abusive work conditions given H-1B holders’ dependence on retaining their employment in order to avoid removal back to their country of origin."

FURY ERUPTS AS US BRAND FIRES 1,600 EMPLOYEES AFTER SECURING THOUSANDS OF FOREIGN WORKER VISAS

He said the alleged fraud is sowing uncertainty in the U.S. labor market by undercutting wages and unfairly increasing competition for American workers, particularly those fresh out of college.

"Bad actors have developed illicit methods for meeting the requirements for obtaining H-1B visas and the necessary work authorizations, and they employ these methods at scale to enrich themselves through fraud and exploitation via the most threadbare compliance with the letter of the law," McCormick wrote.

VICE PRESIDENT VANCE SAYS MIGRANT COMMUNITIES SHOW 'CLEAR PATTERN' IN FEDERAL FRAUD AS INVESTIGATIONS WIDEN

The Georgia Republican said his suspicions were raised by "stakeholder engagement, reports from my constituents, and recent federal investigation and enforcement activity targeting entities in and around GA-07."

And while he did not name specific businesses or people he believes are associated with such fraud, McCormick argued, "Metro Atlanta’s recent economic growth and international airport unfortunately make it a logical area of concentration for these bad actors."

EXCLUSIVE: ‘PHANTOM EMPLOYEES' SCANDAL SPURS GOP CRACKDOWN ON $36B INCENTIVE FOR COMPANIES TO BYPASS AMERICANS

The Trump administration launched an investigation into suspected H-1B visa fraud in July.

H-1B visas have become the subject of fierce debate on the right, with prominent critics like Vice President JD Vance calling it a "broken" system while calling to eliminate it altogether.

Supporters of H-1B visas, like Elon Musk and Vivek Ramaswamy, have argued it's critical for attracting global talent in fields like technology and engineering that are key to keeping the U.S. at the forefront of global innovation.

item.title: Coco Gauff calls out 'insane' racist comments after 16-year-old opponent gets emotional following controversy
item.description: Coco Gauff fired back at racist comments after a controversial point replay against Sun Xinran at the China Open sparked online backlash.
item.content:encoded:
Coco Gauff found herself in some controversy in her match at the China Open against 16-year-old Sun Xinran, who was playing on home soil.

Gauff stopped a rally after electronic advertising boards lining the court flickered during a point late in the first set of her 7-5, 6-1 third-round victory over Xinran, a 16-year-old who recently won the U.S. Open junior title.

Sun appeared about to win the point when Gauff stopped playing, but the chair umpire then ordered the point to be replayed.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Gauff explained what occurred in the moment, but not before replying to a post on X calling her a racial slur.

"hey everyone, you can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist. the amount of racist comments/dms I’ve received in the last few hours is insane," Gauff said, adding that she is "not a cheater or a thief."

Gauff has called out racism in the past, saying she received similar comments from gamblers earlier this year.

Gauff then said that she saw a light "flicker" early on in the point "but was not sure if that is what I actually saw."

"We are told before the matches we are allowed to continue to finish play so KEEP IT (sic) MIND i am thinking about all of this while i’m playing the point. anything can be challenged after the point is over... If I would’ve lost the point my opponent is also free to do the same thing and ask for a replay and she would’ve have been completely in her right to do so," Gauff explained.

Gauff said she saw the light flicker again and raised her hands.

PATRICK MCENROE ON U.S. OPEN WEED SMELL, TRANS ATHLETES, FOREIGN RECRUITS RESHAPING COLLEGE TENNIS

"It was an unfortunate situation but it is out of my control, the think pieces and calling me an unfair is ridiculous when those are the rules. I did not make them, I think it’s weird i’m getting hate for following the rules," Gauff said.

"Xinran is incredible talent and player, I apologized for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood."

Sun, who was given a wild-card entry by tournament organizers and was making her WTA Tour debut, appeared distraught after the loss. Gauff, who reached the fourth round of Wimbledon as a 15-year-old in 2019, sympathized with Sun.

"I did not like to see her so emotional as I’ve been there and I really understand what it is like but this is just the beginning of an incredible career. It was an honor to share the court in front of her home crowd."

Gauff will now play in the round of 16 on Wednesday against Elise Mertens.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Yoshinobu Yamamoto vs Chris Sale in pivotal NLDS Game 3 as Dodgers and Braves meet tied 1-1
item.description: Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Chris Sale duel in a pivotal National League Division Series Game 3 with the Dodgers and Braves tied 1-1 in the series.
item.content:encoded:
It is hard to believe that we are already at the middle mark of the National League Division Series. Winners of Game 3 of the series go on to win about 72% of the time when teams come into the match tied 1-1. I don't think many more words need to be written to state the importance of this game. That is the situation facing the Dodgers and Braves today. It isn't a death sentence by any means, but one team will move forward with their backs against the wall, and another will be in a bit more control.

The Los Angeles Dodgers have been one of the best teams in baseball for years. They've won the past two World Series, they've gotten big name after big name and they continue to push to keep winning more trophies. Every fan should want their team to be like the Dodgers. A season after winning the World Series for the second straight year, they went out and signed the best closer available — a weakness for the team — and the best hitter available. Not only that, but they went out and traded for the best pitcher on the market, Tarik Skubal.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Investing in your team is what should be done, not something other franchises should be jealous of. Prior to the additions this year, they've obviously added key pieces to help them nab two World Series trophies. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who starts this evening for them, is one addition who certainly helped last season. He took home the World Series MVP trophy and was arguably their best player in the entire postseason. He allowed just six earned runs over 37.1 innings, including two complete games and a major stretch Game 7. Braves hitters haven't done all that well against Yamamoto, batting just .196 over 51 at-bats.

The Atlanta Braves had a down season last year, but came back with vengeance this year. For all intents and purposes, they led the National League East for the entire season. Sure, the Phillies may have taken a lead briefly, but they couldn't hold on to it the way that Atlanta did. It is actually a bit surprising they've been this successful, considering their pitching staff has suffered all sorts of injuries this year. Those who are available have seemed to step up.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Tonight, the guy who has been most reliable, Chris Sale, is taking the mound for the Braves in this pivotal game. Sale in the postseason has appeared in two games, going 7.2 innings, allowing five hits, and striking out 12 hitters. Sale pitched in Game 1 for the Braves, going six innings. He also threw in Game 3 on short rest, but today would be normal rest for him. Most Dodgers hitters have struggled against Sale in his career. Mookie Betts has been good against him, but without him, the Dodgers are 21-for-122.

This is probably as close to a pick'em as you're going to get in the playoffs. That's what happens when you get two great teams facing off. The Braves are 23 games above .500 at home, but the Dodgers are no slouches on the road. I honestly believe this game could go either way, but I feel like the Dodgers are the correct side. Most of this is because Sale had to throw in Game 3, and I do think that can alter his rest a bit, even with the time between then and now. Yamamoto seems to be a big-game pitcher as well. Give me Los Angeles.

item.title: DNA testing confirms body of flight attendant who was killed and thrown from bridge
item.description: Dennis Day allegedly admitted to strangling Rana Nofal Soluri and dumping her body off a Texas bridge, but DNA testing now links him to the remains.
item.content:encoded:
Authorities announced that DNA testing identified a body found in a Texas creek as a missing flight attendant whose roommate has been charged with killing her and dumping her remains off a bridge.

Rana Nofal Soluri, 47, was found on June 13 by a fisherman on the bank of Brushy Creek under a bridge in Montague County, about 70 miles northwest of Fort Worth, according to police and local reports. The remains were taken to the University of North Texas Health’s Center for Human Identification, where DNA testing recently confirmed the identity as Soluri, a Fort Worth Police Department spokesperson told NBC News.

Soluri worked for Envoy Air, a regional carrier owned by American Airlines, and had been missing since March 2025. She had taken time off for a minor operation and was expected to return to work on March 31, 2025, but a co-worker reported her missing months later, on June 11, 2025, after she failed to return and could not be reached, police said.

TERROR CELLS INSIDE FOREIGN AIRLINES 'CERTAINLY A POSSIBILITY,' RETIRED PILOT WARNS

Dennis Day, 67, Soluri’s former roommate and longtime friend, was arrested in June 2025 and charged with murder. Police said Day admitted he "snapped" during a dispute with Soluri before he "began to strangle her with his bare hands," according to an arrest warrant cited by reports.

Day allegedly told investigators he strangled Soluri on the kitchen floor, dragged her body into the backyard, loaded her "head first" into a large black trash bin and transported her body roughly 70 miles away before dumping it over a bridge, according to court documents.

Investigators said home surveillance video from Day’s Fort Worth house showed him dragging "what appears to be a lifeless body from the home into the backyard" on March 21, 2025. Police also said an "inadvertent call" and message on another woman’s phone captured a panicked Day asking for help moving Soluri’s body.

FLORIDA JUDGE RIPS INTO MOM ACCUSED OF LEAVING 4 CHILDREN AT HOME TO GO ON 3-DAY CRUISE

That woman, identified as Joni Thomas, also known as Joanne Walters, 63, was charged with tampering with evidence with intent to impair a human corpse. Police allege that she helped Day dispose of Soluri’s body. Both cases remain pending.

Before the DNA confirmation, prosecutors said Day had bragged to people in jail that he could not be convicted if authorities never found Soluri’s body, according to a notice filed by the Tarrant County Criminal District Attorney’s Office and cited by the Fort Worth Star-Telegram.

A GoFundMe page set up for Soluri’s daughter, Lulu Soluri, said American Airlines helped fly her mother’s remains to Seattle for a Muslim burial, which took place on Sept. 29. The fundraiser said Lulu also plans to travel to Texas for a future court date, where she is expected to deliver a statement.

"Lulu is a very private person, so this is a huge feat for her to face the person accused of killing her mother," the GoFundMe read. "Lulu thanks everyone for their support. She is always overwhelmed knowing how many people have helped her during this process."

item.title: How to search anything on iPhone, Galaxy and Pixel
item.description: Apple's iOS 27 Visual Intelligence now lets your iPhone search objects directly on screen, but Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel have a head start.
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever spotted a great pair of shoes in a video and wondered where to buy them? Maybe someone sent you a photo of a restaurant, plant or gadget, and you wanted to know more without typing a description into Google.

Apple's newly released iOS 27 gives iPhone owners an easier way to do that. Visual Intelligence can now understand what's already displayed on your screen, so you can search an object, ask a question about it or take action based on what your iPhone sees. Apple says you can even turn information from a flyer or invitation into a calendar event.

Samsung Galaxy and Google Pixel owners have a similar tool through Google's Circle to Search. Instead of switching apps, you can select something directly on your screen and immediately search for more information.

Here's how all three work and where you'll find the controls on the latest software.

8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare with AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed.

Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist.

Watch the free replays and get your checklists at CyberGuyLive.com.

Visual Intelligence previously focused heavily on things around you. You could point your iPhone camera at something and use Apple Intelligence to identify it or search for more information. iOS 27 expands that experience to content already displayed on your iPhone. Take a screenshot and Visual Intelligence can offer tools based on what it recognizes. Apple says those options can include visual search, questions about the screen, text summaries, Read Aloud and actions such as adding an event to Calendar.

That opens up some useful possibilities. Say you're watching a video and notice a lamp you like in the background. You can pause the video, take a screenshot and search for something similar instead of trying to describe the lamp yourself. You could also receive a digital event flyer in Messages. Rather than switching to Calendar and manually entering the details, Visual Intelligence may recognize the event information and give you an option to add it.

That's the big reason we're looking at this feature now. iOS 27 brings Apple's visual search much deeper into what you're already doing on the iPhone. If you recently installed Apple's latest update, you'll also want to check out our article on 10 iOS 27 features you'll want to try now.

One thing to keep straight is that an iPhone can support iOS 27 without supporting Visual Intelligence. Apple Intelligence on iOS 27 requires an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max or iPhone 16 model or later. Availability can also vary by language and region. Meanwhile, iOS 27 itself works on many older iPhones. So, if you installed iOS 27 on an older supported iPhone and don't see these Visual Intelligence tools, your phone may simply lack the hardware needed for Apple Intelligence.

This is the new part I think many iPhone owners will want to try first.

The available buttons change based on what's inside the screenshot, so don't expect every option to appear each time. I like that Apple built this around the screenshot process because most iPhone owners already know how to do that. You don't have to learn an entirely new gesture before you can start experimenting.

On a supported iPhone, Visual Intelligence can use the camera to help you learn more about what's in front of you. Apple says you can search for similar images, get details about a business, translate or summarize text and identify certain plants and animals. If your iPhone has Camera Control, one of the quickest ways to use Visual Intelligence is to press and hold Camera Control. Then point your iPhone at whatever caught your attention and choose from the options that appear.

There's also a newer option in iOS 27 if you turn on Siri AI. Open the Camera app and tap Siri to switch to Siri mode. From there, you can ask questions, search based on what's in the camera frame or take suggested actions. Siri AI is still officially in beta and availability depends on your device, language and region. I like this camera side of Visual Intelligence because you don't have to know exactly what you're looking at before you search for it. Point your iPhone at something that interests you, then let the phone help you figure out what to ask next.

APPLE AI SECURITY UPDATE PROVES HACKERS MOVE FAST

Samsung Galaxy owners may already be familiar with Google's Circle to Search. The feature arrived on Galaxy devices before Apple's new iOS 27 screen-search capability and remains available across a growing number of compatible phones and tablets.

According to Samsung, Circle to Search works on select Galaxy devices running Android 14 with One UI 6.1 or later. The company began rolling out its newer One UI 9 software in September 2026, but you do not need One UI 9 to use Circle to Search.

One advantage is that you don't have to take a screenshot first. Instead, you can activate Circle to Search directly over whatever you're already viewing on the screen.

First, make sure Circle to Search is enabled.

Go to Settings > Display > Navigation bar, then make sure Circle to Search is turned on.

Then:

Circle to Search can also work while the Camera app is open on supported Galaxy devices. Point your camera at something, then use the same Home button or navigation handle method to open Circle to Search and select what you want to investigate. That can be especially useful when you're looking at something in a store or trying to identify an object without taking a photo first.

What if Circle to Search isn't working on your Galaxy?

Start with the simplest check.

Go to Settings > Display > Navigation bar and make sure Circle to Search is turned on. You should also keep your phone software and Google app updated.

If you see a message saying search isn't available because of your settings, go to Settings > Apps > Choose default apps > Digital assistant app and check whether Analyze on-screen images is enabled.

Keep in mind that some apps can block screen capture or analysis for security or copyright reasons. Circle to Search may not work inside those apps.

Google Pixel phones use the same underlying Circle to Search feature, although some capabilities can vary by model. Google currently supports Circle to Search on Pixel 6 and later. Like on Galaxy, you can search something already displayed on your Pixel without leaving the app.

ANDROID MALWARE CAN STEAL YOUR PIN AND BANK LOGINS

Before trying the gesture, make sure Circle to Search is turned on. Go to Settings and use the search bar at the top to search for Circle to Search. Tap the result, then make sure the feature is enabled.

If Circle to Search still does not work, go to Settings > Apps > Default apps > Digital assistant app. Make sure Google is selected as your digital assistant and that Use screen and app data is turned on. Google also recommends keeping the Google app updated.

Then:

You can also adjust your selection by dragging its borders. Google lets you add words to your search for more specific results, and Circle to Search can translate content on the screen, too.

If nothing happens when you press and hold the navigation handle or Home button, try Circle to Search on your Home screen, Chrome or a photo in Google Photos. Some apps can block screen capture or screen analysis, which can prevent the feature from appearing.

Shopping is probably the most obvious example. You might see a jacket in an Instagram video or a chair in someone's living room photo. Instead of trying to come up with the perfect search terms, you can select what you're looking at and let your phone do the visual searching. Travel can be another useful situation. Maybe someone sends you a photo of a landmark you don't recognize or you see a restaurant in a video from a city you're visiting. Visual search can help you identify it and start digging into the details.

Text may be even more useful. Circle to Search can copy and translate text without making you jump between apps. On iPhone, Visual Intelligence can recognize text and may offer actions based on what it sees, such as summarizing it or creating a calendar event. I would still double-check anything important. Visual search results can identify the wrong object or show you something that only looks similar. Think of these tools as a fast way to start searching rather than a guarantee that the first answer is correct.

This is worth thinking about because these tools can see content that you intentionally select from your screen. Apple says many Apple Intelligence requests run directly on the device. More complex requests can use Private Cloud Compute. Apple says data sent to Private Cloud Compute is used to fulfill the request and is not retained by that system afterward.

Apple also gives iOS 27 users Visual Intelligence controls under Settings > Siri. Depending on your setup, those controls can include options related to Visual Intelligence and visual search.

Google says Circle to Search activity can be saved with your other Google Search activity. Search history and personalization controls can affect how that information is handled.

I would be selective about using visual search on highly sensitive screens. Banking information, medical records, passwords or private documents are poor places to experiment with any cloud-connected search feature.

We've also taken a closer look at AI privacy and security in our article Is Apple Intelligence on your iPhone really secure?

I like features that save me from trying to describe something I can already see. If there's a watch, plant, restaurant or piece of furniture right in front of me, I would much rather point at it or select it than play a guessing game with search terms. Galaxy and Pixel owners have had a head start with Circle to Search, and Google's approach remains very fast. Hold the control at the bottom of the screen, select what caught your eye and you're searching. Apple's iOS 27 update now gives supported iPhone owners a much more capable way to do something similar through Visual Intelligence. What interests me most about Apple's approach is what happens after the iPhone recognizes something. Searching for a product is useful, but turning an invitation into a calendar event or summarizing text can save additional steps. That's where these tools start feeling like something you may actually use instead of a feature you try once and forget. I would still keep one healthy habit: check the result before trusting it. These tools can be impressively fast, but a confident-looking answer can still be wrong.

Would you be comfortable letting your phone analyze almost anything on your screen if it saved you time, or are there some things you would never want Visual Intelligence or Circle to Search looking at? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: White executive fired after wearing cornrows, triggering legal fight over Maryland's CROWN Act
item.description: Attorney Jeremy Eldridge said Maryland's CROWN Act could apply after the Baltimore Rock Opera Society fired a White executive over wearing cornrows.
item.content:encoded:
A White Baltimore arts executive was fired in September from the Baltimore Rock Opera Society after backlash over her decision to wear cornrows following a trip to Burning Man.

Attorney Jeremy Eldridge said the circumstances of the firing of Kelly Carnes could raise discrimination questions under Maryland's CROWN Act. Eldridge said the organization’s public statements about Carnes' hairstyle could become relevant evidence if she challenges her dismissal.

"Had the Baltimore Rock Opera simply separated from this individual without providing a discriminatory reason, the timeline would be all of the evidence that the fired employee would have," he told WBFF Fox45 Baltimore. "But here, when you're making comments publicly that lean into the discriminatory allegation made by the fired employees, that itself could be evidence of the fact that you were terminated wrongfully, meaning that it's discrimination under the CROWN."

WHITE DEVELOPER SUES BALTIMORE MAYOR, CITY COUNCIL CLAIMING HE WAS FIRED BECAUSE OF HIS RACE

Carnes directed Fox News Digital to WBFF's reporting when contacted about the controversy. She began serving as executive director of the Baltimore Rock Opera Society, known as BROS, on Sept. 8. The organization formally announced her appointment less than a week later, touting her more than 21 years of experience in arts leadership, nonprofit strategy, communications, fundraising and operations.

Carnes said she had her hair put into cornrows as a protective hairstyle while attending Burning Man in Nevada’s desert. After she returned, a video showing her with the hairstyle at a BROS event prompted complaints that a White woman wearing cornrows constituted cultural appropriation.

BROS publicly acknowledged the backlash after removing the video, saying it had received concerns from members of its community and was taking the matter seriously. The organization also said it regretted removing the video without an explanation.

"We have received many heartfelt and concerned messages from members of our community regarding a video circulated on social media showing our new Executive Director, who is White, wearing cornrows at a recent BROS public event," the organization said, according to WBAL. "We share the weight of these concerns and take this matter seriously."

WASHINGTON POST ORDERED TO REINSTATE COLUMNIST KAREN ATTIAH AFTER BEING TERMINATED OVER CHARLIE KIRK POSTS

The organization said it would revise its anti-discrimination policy to address cultural representation and dress, require anti-racism leadership training and create a working group focused on racial equity and inclusion, according to The Baltimore Banner.

Carnes said the board advised her not to attend a town hall convened to discuss the controversy. She said she was dismissed days later and was told only that she was "not a good fit."

Eldridge said determining whether the firing violated Maryland law would require establishing what actually motivated the organization’s decision.

"In evaluating whether the CROWN Act applies, meaning whether there was discrimination and whether this individual was terminated for a discriminatory reason because of a hairstyle, we still have to deal with there are two competing narratives," Eldridge said.

NEW YORK TIMES SUED BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT OVER ALLEGED 'DEI-RELATED' EMPLOYMENT DISCRIMINATION

Maryland enacted its CROWN Act in 2020. State law now defines race for purposes of anti-discrimination protections to include "traits associated with race," including hair texture, Afro hairstyles and protective hairstyles. "Protective hairstyles" under the statute include braids, twists and locks.

The Maryland Commission on Civil Rights says the law applies to employment practices including hiring, workplace conditions, discipline and termination. Fox News Digital reached out to the commission for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

The statute does not itself resolve whether Carnes' firing was unlawful, leaving the circumstances and motivation behind the termination central to any potential discrimination claim.

The turmoil has extended beyond Carnes' departure. Four of BROS’ six board members, including its chair, are expected to leave the organization at the end of the year, according to an email obtained by The Baltimore Banner.

A BROS spokesperson separately told WBAL that the organization was focused on caring for its internal community and declined further comment on Carnes’ dismissal.

item.title: Travel nightmare unfolds as major airline scraps flight after harrowing 12-hour delay
item.description: United Airlines Flight 884 from Washington Dulles to Rome was canceled after nearly 12 hours of delays caused by mechanical issues and thunderstorms.
item.content:encoded:
Passengers on a United Airlines flight from Washington, D.C., to Rome on Oct. 2 faced a grueling overnight ordeal as they waited nearly 12 hours to take off — only to have the airline cancel the flight before it left the ground.

United Airlines Flight 884 was scheduled to depart Washington Dulles International Airport at 5:35 p.m. on Oct. 2 for an overnight trip to Rome's Fiumicino Airport.

Instead, passengers were grounded by a cascading series of issues, including a cockpit malfunction, severe thunderstorms and crew changes, "The Aviation Hub" blog reported.

'WE NEED TO RETURN IMMEDIATELY,' FLIGHT CREW WARNS AS PILOT HEALTH EMERGENCY UNFOLDS

"United flight 884 from Washington Dulles to Rome returned to the gate after taxiing to take on additional fuel for a longer planned flight due to weather," United Airlines told Fox News Digital in a statement.

"During this time, a new crew was brought in and a maintenance issue that arose was resolved. The aircraft then pushed back from the gate, but then required another mechanical inspection," the airline's statement continued.

"The flight was then canceled due to crew time limits. We rebooked customers on an extra flight that departed on Saturday evening," the statement concluded.

A faulty door seal and mishap with the plane's pushback tug likely also played a part in the delays, according to the "Simple Flying" aviation blog.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

The problems weren't over, however.

When the flight was canceled at around 4 a.m. the following morning, some of the travelers had been facing delays for 12 hours, Men's Journal noted.

Then, after technical issues, there were thunderstorms. 

The plane sat on the tarmac, waiting to depart. The Boeing 777-200ER returned to the gate around three hours later to refuel, according to several reports.

Ultimately, the passengers had to exit the aircraft because the first crew reached its legal duty-time limit after a six-hour delay. 

A new crew started, but subsequent mechanical issues forced everyone to deplane a second time before the flight was finally canceled.

The affected passengers were finally rebooked on another flight that took off from Dulles just before 7 p.m. on Saturday, putting them en route to Rome over 25 hours later than originally planned.

A frustrated passenger vented in the United Airlines MileagePlus Experts group on Facebook.

"I’m surprised there hasn’t been a mutiny," wrote the passenger, who was on the flight.

"You should be eligible for compensation if you have a traveler's credit card. These things happen. That's why there's insurance," another Facebook user responded.

Not everyone was sympathetic.

"I fly a lot also. If you can’t handle the problems, you have three choices. Fly private, fly a different [airline], don’t fly. I have been flying for 43 years with United. There are ups and downs, live with them or move on," the Facebook user said.

Yet another United flyer said, "Most of the issues you point out are regulations written in blood. … I’d rather not have to relearn them at the risk of safety."

item.title: Richard Gere confronts Hollywood fame, ego and greed as 'dark clouds' that threaten inner peace
item.description: Richard Gere reveals how more than 40 years of practicing Buddhism helps him battle ego, greed and jealousy in his decades-long Hollywood career.
item.content:encoded:
Richard Gere has spent decades in Hollywood, but he hasn’t let fame go to his head — at least not without a fight.

The actor serves as an executive producer of the documentary "Wisdom of Happiness," which explores the Dalai Lama’s teachings and the pursuit of lasting joy. Gere has practiced Buddhism for more than 40 years.

Asked how he keeps fame and ego in check after decades in Hollywood, Gere admitted he isn’t immune.

TIM ROBBINS TURNS TO AYAHUASCA AFTER FEELING 'CONSUMED BY ANGER' OVER CANCEL CULTURE

"Everyone goes through that," the 77-year-old told Fox News Digital. "Everyone has the forces of greed, anger, self-cherishing, impatience, jealousy, the whole gamut. Everyone has that. So I think from Buddhist training and looking at these afflictive emotions and seeing where they’re coming from, they’re not innate in me. They’re kind of add-ons to basic clarity of the mind."

"It’s said that the mind is clear and knowing, so clear, vast, no limits," he said. "It has a sense of knowing, wisdom. The other stuff is just kind of add-ons, like dark clouds coming through. They come, and they go."

Gere also isn’t looking to Hollywood for happiness. The longtime leading man has learned that the perks only go so far.

WATCH: RICHARD GERE SHARES THE LIFE LESSON THAT BRINGS HIM HAPPINESS

"Well, clearly, happiness and peace [don’t] come from the outside," he explained. "It comes from inside all of us, and it’s there. You don’t have to create that. But I think it’s removing the bad habits, removing the causes that make us feel bad ultimately. But we’re in control of our experience for sure. We’re responsible for it. If you don’t like the way things are, you change it. And all things are changeable. They’re changing all the time anyhow. Probably when we fight the change is when we feel the worst."

For Gere, that also means questioning how much material success really matters.

"Well, what’s really important? Is it what I own or what I am?" Gere said. "I’m not going to get anything from the outside that is permanently going to make me happy."

"Momentarily, yes, like a piece of chocolate, but that’s not permanent, is it?" he joked.

Gere has also found happiness far from the spotlight. These days, the star splits his time between Spain and upstate New York.

"Well, Spain is my wife’s country, so she gets super happy there," he said with a smile. "And I’ll tell you when my wife’s super happy, I’m super happy. And I grew up in the Northeast. I feel very close to that. And my early family memories, and my grandfather’s farm in Pennsylvania, I think, had a huge impact. It still does."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Gere and his wife, Spanish publicist Alejandra Silva, have two sons together. Silva also has a son from a previous relationship, while Gere shares his eldest son, Homer, with ex-wife Carey Lowell.

"My first son is 26 now," Gere said. "And I talked to him about what he’s going through right now. And I remember myself as a 25-year-old, 26-year-old person. Of course, my concerns were different. I certainly was more susceptible to what people said and thought about me and about anything else. And frankly, I don’t care that much about it right now, what anyone thinks or says."

Looking back, Gere recalled growing up in "an extraordinary Christian family" with roots in a small town in Pennsylvania. His father, Homer Gere, spent his childhood milking cows, and both his parents instilled in him the importance of helping others — values he carried with him when he discovered Buddhism in his 20s.

"I grew up with that imprint, I think, from my dad and my mom, but there was something about Buddhism that kind of went beyond that and was willing to explore the larger questions," Gere said. "What is reality? What am I? What is a human being?"

"Am I capable of much greater things than just worrying about myself?" he continued. "And certainly, Buddhism wanted to engage those things [for me]."

But the lessons Gere learned from farmers have never left him.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I think that farmers have a balanced sense of the universe," he said. "When the rain doesn’t come, who are you going to complain to? It’s about acceptance of things. It doesn’t make you happy when the rain doesn’t come, or it comes too much, but the forces of the universe are just the way they are. And along with it, hard work."

"Farmers work really hard," Gere said. "I still have the kerosene lantern that my grandfather used. He would get up at four o’clock in the morning and go do the first milking of the cows."

Gere said he sees that same work ethic in the Dalai Lama.

"He still gets up at 3:30 in the morning, does his practice, works on his mind, works on his heart, works on his motivation, purifies himself every day," Gere said.

"He’s a human being, and he continues, as I said, to work on himself," he continued. "If we want to achieve what he’s achieved, to become really such an extraordinary, genuine person, we’ve got to do the work."

Gere said his connection to "Wisdom of Happiness" became deeply personal after he and Silva first watched the film together in New York.

"My wife was in tears," he recalled. "And I thought for his 90th birthday, this would be a great summation of an extraordinary life, well-lived, a meaningful life dedicated to others."

But as the film came together, Gere said its message began to feel increasingly urgent.

"In the time it took to finish the editing and finish the film, I think the world continued to fall apart in a very challenging, dark way," he said.

Gere said he hopes the documentary reminds people they have the capacity for compassion.

"The beginning point, and maybe the end point, is basic kindness, a warm heart and generosity of spirit," he said.

item.content:encoded:
Players sitting on the fence contemplating whether or not to commit to LIV Golf's future will be allowed to sit a bit longer.

LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy in September after the Saudi Public Investment Fund – the sole funder of the league since its inception in 2022 – made the decision to withdraw all financial support at the end of the 2026 season. "Giving players real and actionable ownership in the league and the teams is a unique opportunity in professional golf, and it aligns everyone around the long-term success of the product for the game and for the fans."

item.title: Millions saved by blocking dead people payouts as Trump Treasury drops hammer on federal fraud
item.description: Treasury's "Do Not Pay" program screened over 1.1 billion payments worth $3.7 trillion, catching 13,500 improper payments to deceased people.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: The Treasury Department blocked $175 million in federal payments tied to deceased recipients in fiscal year 2026, up sharply from the $99 million identified just months earlier as the Trump administration expanded government-wide screening for improper payments.

"I applaud Secretary [Scott] Bessent for slamming the door on these fraudsters before they can pick taxpayers’ pockets," Republican Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy told Fox News Digital.

"Unless you were playing Frisbee in the quad during Econ 101, you know the federal government shouldn’t be sending taxpayer money to dead people," Kennedy went on. "I fought for years to pass my common-sense bill to stop fraudsters from gaming the system, and now it’s the law."

Kennedy has for years pushed to give Treasury greater access to Social Security death records, helping pass a 2020 law that temporarily authorized the Social Security Administration to share its full Death Master File with the department. That three-year data-sharing program began in December 2023. Trump then signed Kennedy’s Ending Improper Payments to Deceased People Act into law in February 2026, making access permanent.

TRUMP'S WAR ON FRAUD EXPANDS AS TREASURY LAUNCHES NEW SITE WITH WHISTLEBLOWER INCENTIVES

Trump has tasked his administration with rooting out fraud, waste and abuse across the federal government and tightening safeguards around taxpayer dollars — the latest effort to stop federal benefit payments to dead people is just another initiative within that broader effort.

"President Trump continues to deliver for Americans where previous administrations have fallen short. This Administration is setting new standards in record time to prevent fraud and improper payments before hard-earned taxpayer dollars leave the Treasury. Under President Trump’s leadership, there is no tolerance for waste, fraud, and abuse," White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital.

Treasury screened more than 1.1 billion federal payments totaling roughly $3.7 trillion in FY2026, identifying and returning about 13,500 payments worth $175 million that otherwise would have been distributed to individuals no longer eligible for payments due to death.

"Treasury continues to transform how the federal government protects taxpayer dollars by using better data, stronger controls, and advanced technology to stop fraud and improper payments before money goes out the door," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a press release shared with Fox News Digital.

"In the past year alone, Treasury built and deployed new safeguards that verified more than $3.7 trillion in federal payments and increased Do Not Pay access from 4 percent of programs to 99 percent, ensuring agencies have access to the data they need," Bessent added. "We are moving beyond ‘pay and chase’ and making prevention the federal government’s first line of defense."

WHITE HOUSE PUSHES 'WATERSHED' FRAUD-FIGHTING REFORM IN CONGRESS AS VANCE CONVENES TASK FORCE

More than 99% of federal programs now have access to the "Do Not Pay" tool, up from roughly 4% at the end of FY2025.

The expansion fulfills key requirements of a March 2025 executive order from Trump directing his administration to strengthen safeguards against fraud, waste and abuse involving federal payments.

Treasury also screened more than 2.3 billion records against Do Not Pay data sources in FY2026, nearly four times the 641 million records screened the previous fiscal year.

The jump comes as the program has expanded across the federal government, alongside new payment verification efforts and additional screenings for states.

VANCE TO HOST CONGRESS AT WHITE HOUSE TO DISCUSS LEGISLATIVE ACTION ON FRAUD

Treasury also tested new safeguards aimed at verifying that bank accounts belong to the intended recipients and checking Taxpayer Identification Numbers tied to federal payments.

The checks became fully operational Sept. 30 and allow Treasury to flag and return payments that fail verification before the money is sent.

The latest figures build on Treasury’s July announcement that it had screened more than 885 million payments worth roughly $2.77 trillion and flagged more than 4,900 payments worth about $99 million tied to deceased recipients.

item.title: China’s long-term finances are all wet as bill to maintain huge navy comes due in 2031
item.description: Xi Jinping's navy faces a sustainment wall by 2031 as maintenance costs collide with China's cracking fiscal system and collapsing land sales.
item.content:encoded:
China’s recent state visit bought two months of trade peace. But it did not buy Beijing time on the fleet it has already launched and will soon be unable to afford.

Chinese President Xi Jinping walked a red carpet in Washington for his first state visit to the United States in more than a decade. President Donald Trump greeted him at Joint Base Andrews. There were troop reviews, a state dinner, pandas, an artificial intelligence (AI) "dialogue" and a two-month extension of a trade truce now set to expire Jan. 10. Xi told the cameras the two powers "should coexist in peace." He also pressed Trump to handle Taiwan with "prudence" and oppose independence.

On the minerals that make missiles, drones and warships work, Beijing’s readout went silent. The White House said only that the two sides would "continue to work on" rare-earth shortages — practically meaning America will press hard to address its supply vulnerabilities.

TRUMP-XI REUNION COMES WITH UNFINISHED BUSINESS — AND A BIGGER BATTLE LOOMING

Beyond the pleasantries in Washington — it costs little to be polite and talk is far cheaper than war — China continues to press forward on a war footing, launching warships at a breathtaking pace.

Communist China’s problem is no longer whether it can build a navy. It built one. The problem is whether it can keep one after 2031.

IS THE US ALREADY LOSING TO CHINA ON INNOVATION, LOGISTICS AND RAPID RESUPPLY?

Procurement is the cheap year. Operations and maintenance are not cheap. For a modern navy, operating and support costs commonly consume 60% to 70% of a ship’s life-cycle cost. The People’s Liberation Army Navy spent a decade in series production: destroyers, frigates, carriers, conventional and nuclear submarines. But if overhaul rates on these new ships resemble the old ones, the heaviest work on China’s most capable surface combatants begins around 2031 and runs for a decade. This will force repair yards to compete with new-build demand. The maintenance workforce is already stretched. Fuel, munitions and realistic training hours add considerably to the cost.

That bill lands on a fiscal system already cracking at the local level. In 21 provincial-level regions, local revenue covers less than half of spending. Land sales, the main source of provincial income, have collapsed. Beijing has spent two years swapping "hidden" local debt onto official books, which lowered interest rates and raised the visible pile. Interest is now a hard claim on weak cash flow. Beijing can still issue bonds and order state banks to roll paper. But it cannot restore 2010s’ growth or a healthy property market. Deflation makes every yuan of debt heavier.

History has seen this movie. In the 1930s, German Minister of the Economy Hjalmar Schacht hid Nazi rearmament behind Mefo bills — phony promissory notes a shell company issued so the official deficit looked respectable — and stayed hidden from the requirements of the Versailles treaty. By late 1938, the trick was exhausted. The first bills were coming due. Schacht warned that arms spending would have to be cut or the Reich would go broke. Adolf Hitler fired him. What kept Germany solvent afterward was loot: Austria, then Czechoslovakia’s gold and Skoda arms works, then Poland. Plunder postponed insolvency.

Xi is not running a Mefo scheme. Local-government financing vehicles were built to pave roads and hit GDP targets, not to conceal a Versailles-illegal Wehrmacht. The parallel that matters is the maturity date. A built force starts to demand a flow of money the buildup years did not require. Hitler could rob neighbors. Xi cannot cash a Czech National Bank. He can try coercion, blockade or a short, violent fait accompli against Taiwan before the sustainment wall arrives — and before American industry finishes rerouting the supply chains his predecessors spent 20 years capturing.

CHINA’S GRIP ON RARE-EARTH MAGNETS COULD CRUSH US DRONE INDUSTRY BEFORE IT GROWS

That is why China’s rare-earth squeeze play looks early.

China still refines the overwhelming share of the magnets used inside U.S. and allied weapons. Beijing tightened licenses, then blacklisted American firms standing up mines and magnet plants. The concept aimed to freeze the West’s rearmament while the PLA finished its own. But Trump treated the squeeze as the warning it was. Capital has rapidly moved to address the supply chain vulnerability. The Pentagon is pushing Chinese magnets out of defense supply chains, rendering America far less helpless by 2031 than it was in 2024. Every year Xi waits to use this new navy, China’s chokehold on America weakens.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The recent pageantry should not confuse anyone. Xi asked Washington to go quiet on Taiwan, yet earned no policy change. He offered no real minerals deal. He settled for a two-month extension and a photo under the chandeliers. The Chinese Communist Party has centralized power, purged the officer corps and launched a modern and massive fleet — one that will be increasingly expensive to keep in five years.

Peace through strength is imperative to maintain deterrence. Time is the commodity Xi is running out of. America should spend the next five years as if he knows it.

item.title: Fox News Power Rankings: The biggest surprises come after October
item.description: Democrats play defense in Minnesota and New Hampshire while Republicans spend big in Arkansas, Mississippi, and Idaho ahead of the midterms.
item.content:encoded:
Four weeks out from the election, and for most Americans, it’s time for football, foliage and flannel. For politics watchers, all eyes are on an October surprise.

They’ve been game-changers before. In 2008, the collapse of Lehman Brothers, which ushered in the biggest financial crisis since the Great Depression, was a turning point in John McCain’s presidential campaign. He was even with Barack Obama when the news broke, then trailed in every survey after. He lost the popular vote by seven points.

Surprises have come from home and abroad. In 1980, it was President Jimmy Carter’s inability to resolve the Iranian hostage crisis. Eight years earlier, it was President Richard Nixon’s announcement that "peace was at hand" in Vietnam.

Some have more impact than others. It’s not clear that news about George W. Bush’s DUI changed much about the 2000 election, nor that James Comey’s letter to Congress about Hillary Clinton’s email server was the decider in President Trump’s 2016 win.

Still, these surprises all have one thing in common: they happened in presidential years.

EXPLOSIVE SLEEPER ISSUE COULD FUEL MIDTERM SHAKEUPS, TOP REPUBLICAN PREDICTS: ‘YOU’RE GONNA SEE SURPRISES’

It’s not as though we don’t get breaking news during the last month of a midterm cycle. Take 2018, when the GOP warned about a migrant caravan, Brett Kavanaugh sought a seat on the Supreme Court, and a gunman opened fire at a Pittsburgh synagogue.

But that was the exception, not the rule. For the most part, midterm October surprises affect individual races, not the overall trajectory of a party.

In the last midterm, for example, Herschel Walker faced damaging allegations about paying for former girlfriends’ abortions, while in Florida, the destruction caused by Hurricane Ian gave Gov. Ron DeSantis the opportunity to show Floridians that he could be trusted to handle a crisis.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: FOR THE DEMOCRATS, WHERE COULD IT POSSIBLY GO WRONG?

Voters haven’t changed their minds about Trump or the party they’d prefer to elect to the House for several months now, so local stories like these are the ones to watch in the final weeks of the campaign.

Besides, the biggest surprises come after October.

For what still looks like a good – maybe great – year for the Democrats, the party is playing defense in some unexpected places.

DAVID MARCUS: IN DEEP BLUE MINNESOTA A RED DAWN MAY BE RISING AHEAD OF THE MIDTERMS

That starts with Minnesota, where Republicans have a star candidate in Michele Tafoya. The former NFL sideline reporter has been up and down the state with a message to "stop the fraud" if elected to the Senate. That’s been a hot issue in the state, and it’s allowed her to target the Democrat, Peggy Flanagan, who currently serves as lieutenant governor.

Then there’s New Hampshire, another state where Democrats are in the driver’s seat thanks to this political environment, but where the GOP has a favorable match up. Former U.S. Senator John E. Sununu is back on the ballot this year against Chris Pappas, who seems to have had trouble animating his voters.

Even Oregon’s gubernatorial race is competitive this year.

Meanwhile, Republicans are spending money in surprising places.

REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY.

In Arkansas, Sen. Tom Cotton has thrown $13.6 million at his reelection bid, outspending his Democratic opponent Hallie Schoffner 65 to 1. Cotton may have ambitions beyond his current role in the Senate, but in 2020, his spending fell short of $1 million.

Idahoans got a letter in the mail from Vice President Vance last month warning them that Democrats could "pour millions of dollars" into independent challenger Todd Achilles; Vance called it an "urgent national race."

Mississippi Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith has been running ads attacking her Democratic challenger Scott Colom in recent weeks, calling him a "failed prosecutor" with a "chilling" record on crime; that state has seen $5 million in ad spending so far this year.

FOX NEWS POLL: IT’S A LONE STAR SENATE SHOWDOWN BETWEEN TALARICO AND PAXTON

And Florida is full of election surprises. In 2018, Rick Scott won his Senate race by 0.1 percentage points while DeSantis won his by 0.4 points. Two years later, the presidential race was decided by just 3.4 points.

Nebraska and South Dakota could be closer-than-expected for Republicans as well.

In this week’s Power Rankings, one Carolina gets more competitive while another drifts away from the GOP, and Democrats get nervous about a governor’s race in Oregon.

The math is the same in the Senate. Each party has 47 seats to their name, leaving six toss-up races to determine control.

Those are Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and Texas, which all look close in the flurry of surveys released by pollsters last week.

Two other races are highly competitive: New Hampshire (Lean D) and Kansas (Lean R).

On the polling alone, these look more like toss-up states: surveys released last week have the Democrat ahead by only five points in New Hampshire, and the Kansas race dead even. It’s the partisan makeup of these states that keeps them at "lean."

North Carolina is less competitive than it was two weeks ago. Fox News confirmed on Friday that the Senate Leadership Fund, a powerful Super PAC aligned with Republican leadership, was pulling resources from the state. Earlier, Sen. Tim Scott left it off a list of states where Republicans were focusing spending.

GOP nominee Michael Whatley is running as strong a race as he can there, and the margin will probably be tighter than polls currently have it. But the Democrat, Roy Cooper, is also a strong candidate, and he has had double-digit leads in multiple surveys.

North Carolina moves from Lean D to Likely D.

Nearby South Carolina is getting more competitive. Darline Graham, appointed to the Senate after the death of her brother, Lindsey, is reportedly getting more help on the campaign trail from President Trump.

There are lingering questions about Graham’s ability to turn out a broad spectrum of Republican voters against a Democratic candidate who, like her counterparts in Kansas and Nebraska, is pushing hard on the price of diesel.

The state moves from Solid R to Likely R.

Four years ago, Oregonians sent Tina Kotek to the governor’s mansion for the first time, and it hasn’t gone smoothly.

Kotek faces four issues all at once in this campaign, as outlined in local reports and on the trail: a housing crisis, poor education outcomes, higher city crime rates than in neighboring states, and like other incumbents, she flip-flopped on data centers.

A lethargic debate performance last week didn’t help matters.

Drazan has lost this race before, and this time, won’t get help from a third-party candidate who drew votes from the Democrat. But this time around, she has created more distance both from Trump and conversations about abortion, which she calls a "settled issue."

Democrats have every reason to hold on to this state in November, but it’s going to be tougher than the party wants. Oregon moves from Likely D to Lean D.

Elsewhere, two states are becoming more competitive for Democrats, beginning with Florida.

The Sunshine State is the home of the "MAGA" movement, and Rep. Byron Donalds easily locked up the Republican nomination in August. But he has stumbled, at times, on the campaign trail, and Hispanic voters continue to express frustration with this economy. Florida moves from Solid R to Likely R.

And in Vermont, longtime incumbent Republican Phil Scott might have raised an eyebrow at a new poll from the University of New Hampshire showing his Democratic opponent, Amanda Janoo, up six points against Scott, 49% to 43%.

Scott keeps winning elections comfortably in Vermont, but the party label could be a bigger problem this cycle. The Green Mountain State also moves from Solid R to Likely R.

item.description: University of Wisconsin-Madison researchers worked on China's vehicle-road-cloud technology that lets roadside cameras track and command vehicles.

FIRST ON FOX: Researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison overlapped on work with China's powerful police ministry developing vehicle technology capable of tracking cars and overtaking driving functions, according to findings from a report shared exclusively with Fox News Digital ahead of its release.

Beijing has already begun deploying the systems across China.

The technology, known as "vehicle-road-cloud" integration, links cars with roadside cameras and sensors and centralized cloud platforms, allowing authorities to monitor traffic in real time and, at its most advanced levels, send commands to connected vehicles.

The implications of connected vehicles have alarmed U.S. officials.

The Commerce Department moved last year to restrict certain Chinese and Russian connected-vehicle technology in the United States, warning that foreign adversaries could potentially collect sensitive information about American drivers or remotely manipulate their cars.

HARVARD, NYU AMONG 30 UNIVERSITIES HIT WITH PENTAGON FOREIGN-TIE AUDIT DEADLINE

In 2016, then-UW Vice Provost Jeffrey Russell traveled to Southeast University, where the schools signed agreements covering research, faculty exchanges, student training and plans to create a joint institute. The following year, Southeast University's president traveled to Madison to formally establish the Joint Research Institute, according to university records cited by Strategy Risks.

The institute focused on intelligent transportation, connected and autonomous vehicles and vehicle-road-cloud technology. UW-Madison's own College of Engineering wrote in 2019 that the institute had "launched in late 2017."

Two years later, UW researchers appeared on technical work that also involved an institute of China's Ministry of Public Security.

Five UW-Madison researchers were among 46 contributors to a Chinese industry report on vehicle-road cooperative automated driving, according to Strategy Risks. The UW-SEU joint institute was listed first among the report's drafting units, while the Traffic Management Research Institute of China's Ministry of Public Security was listed seventh.

The extent of UW-Madison's institutional involvement in the joint institute is disputed.

Counsel for a UW professor told Strategy Risks that the contemplated arrangement was never implemented and that the institute was never operational, funded or staffed by UW. Strategy Risks said it has not independently resolved that dispute, pointing to public records from both universities describing the institute as established.

UW-Madison did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Related vehicle-road-cloud technology was, meanwhile, becoming part of China's national connected-vehicle push.

In 2023, three major Chinese transportation and communications standards bodies published a framework for vehicle-road-cloud integration. Southeast University was among the drafters alongside the Road Traffic Safety Research Center of China's Ministry of Public Security.

The following year, the MPS joined four other Chinese ministries in launching a vehicle-road-cloud pilot program across 20 cities and regional groupings.

OHIO STATE PAYS $2.1M SETTLEMENT AS IT ADMITS RESEARCHER HAD ‘INAPPROPRIATE FOREIGN AFFILIATIONS’ TO CHINA

Under the government plan, participating cities are to install connected roadside equipment and sensing systems and build city-level cloud platforms capable of communicating with vehicles. The platforms can provide information to vehicles and assist with decision-making, planning and control, while safety-monitoring systems track participating vehicles in real time.

Chinese authorities describe the program as an effort to improve traffic safety, advance autonomous driving and accelerate the country's connected-vehicle industry. But those same capabilities have raised security concerns in Washington, where officials have warned that connected-vehicle systems could be exploited to collect sensitive data or remotely manipulate vehicles.

Strategy Risks stressed that it is not accusing UW-Madison of intentionally transferring technology to China's security apparatus.

"Strategy Risks does not allege that UW-Madison, either on its own or through the JRI, deliberately channeled U.S. technology into Chinese surveillance or military systems," the report states.

But the group argues the research nevertheless contributed to technology that later took on broader applications in China.

"The available evidence indicates that research conducted by scholars affiliated with the JRI contributed to the development of a civilian-framed dual-use technology in technical areas that also received U.S. institutional and federal research support," the report states.

"When Beijing incorporated this technology into national standards, the state absorbed a system that has significant surveillance, military, and human rights dimensions."
